conclusion.justification: The report concludes that the evidence regarding hypnosis for smoking cessation is insufficient and inconclusive, explicitly stating that while it cannot definitively rule out an effect, the evidence base is too weak to confidently recommend it as an effective intervention. This fits the definition of a hedged stance.
conclusion.label: hedged

report:
## Conclusion

Your intuition is largely correct, though the evidence is better described as **insufficient/inconclusive** rather than definitively showing "no effect." The most authoritative source—the Cochrane review (2019)—examined 14 studies with 1,926 participants and found **insufficient evidence** that hypnotherapy yields higher six-month quit rates compared to no intervention or other treatments, with pooled risk ratios showing no significant differences (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001008_does-hypnotherapy-help-people-who-are-trying-stop-smoking). An academic summary of that review confirms this finding (https://www.academia.edu/66506574/Hypnotherapy_for_smoking_cessation).

A 2024 randomized controlled trial published in Frontiers reinforced this caution, stating that "the efficacy of hypnotherapy as a tobacco cessation intervention cannot be considered sufficiently proven due to significant methodological limitations in the studies available to date" (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1330362/full).

A 2023 Frontiers meta-analysis found widely varying effect sizes (d = −0.04 to d = 2.72), with only about 29% of reported effects being large and many non-significant (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1330238/full).

Some individual studies and smaller meta-analyses report promising quit rates, but these are generally limited by poor methodological quality. The overall picture: hypnosis *may* help some individuals, but the current evidence base is too weak to confidently recommend it as an effective smoking cessation intervention.
